lessonTitle: Preoperative Risk Assessment: Function, Comorbidity and Fasting

blocks.text: A 72-year-old woman is booked for an elective hip replacement. At the pre-assessment clinic she reports that she has to stop to catch her breath on one flight of stairs, she takes lisinopril, metformin, a beta-blocker and long-term prednisolone, and she mentions she would 'like a late breakfast' on the day. Preoperative assessment turns these ordinary details into a plan that makes the operation safer.

blocks.markdown: **Why assess before anaesthesia?** The aims are to identify and optimise medical conditions, to estimate risk, to plan the anaesthetic and postoperative care (including the level of monitoring and critical care), to give instructions about fasting and medicines, and to obtain informed consent. Assessment is ideally done early, in a pre-assessment clinic for elective patients, so that problems such as anaemia, uncontrolled hypertension, diabetes or sleep apnoea can be addressed before the operation date. It combines history, examination and selected tests; tests should be ordered according to patient and surgical risk and not routinely.

**Airway assessment (objective 1).** The aim is to predict difficulty with facemask ventilation, laryngoscopy and intubation. History includes previous difficulty with anaesthesia, snoring or sleep apnoea, and neck or jaw problems. Examination looks at mouth opening, dentition (loose or prominent upper incisors), the Mallampati class, thyromental distance, mandibular protrusion, neck extension, and body habitus. The Mallampati class is judged with the patient sitting, mouth open and tongue protruded: class I shows the soft palate, uvula, fauces and pillars; class II shows the soft palate, uvula and fauces; class III shows the soft palate and only the base of the uvula; class IV shows only the hard palate. Higher classes predict more difficult laryngoscopy, but no single test is accurate, so tests are combined and a plan is prepared for failure.

**Cardiorespiratory fitness and comorbidity.** Functional capacity is the best simple guide to cardiopulmonary reserve. It is expressed in metabolic equivalents (METs); the ability to climb two flights of stairs or walk up a hill without stopping corresponds to roughly four METs or more and suggests reasonable reserve, whereas inability to do so suggests poor reserve and prompts further assessment, which may include echocardiography or cardiopulmonary exercise testing for major surgery. Specific questions cover chest pain, breathlessness, syncope, palpitations, orthopnoea and oedema, asthma and COPD, diabetes, kidney disease, liver disease, anaemia, anticoagulants and previous anaesthetics. Higher surgical risk and several cardiac risk factors (for example ischaemic heart disease, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, insulin-treated diabetes and renal impairment) increase the chance of postoperative complications.

rows: Airway
Mouth opening, Mallampati class, thyromental distance, neck extension, dentition, previous difficulty
Predicts difficult laryngoscopy and ventilation; plan equipment and expertise
Cardiovascular
Functional capacity (METs), chest pain, heart failure, valve disease, ECG, echocardiography if indicated
Estimates perioperative cardiac risk and haemodynamic reserve
Respiratory
Asthma or COPD control, smoking, sleep apnoea, spirometry where indicated
Risk of postoperative pulmonary complications
Other comorbidity
Diabetes control, renal function, anaemia, anticoagulants, steroids
Optimisation and medicine management
blocks.caption: Principal domains of preoperative assessment.
BMI in kg/m2 where m is body mass in kg and h is height in metres. Obesity affects airway, ventilation, sleep apnoea risk, drug dosing and surgical risk.

blocks.title: Calculating BMI and its implications
blocks.prompt: A patient weighs 92 kg and is 1.60 m tall. Calculate BMI and say why it matters to the anaesthetist.

steps.text: A BMI above 30 kg/m2 is obese. Ask about sleep apnoea and reflux, anticipate difficult mask ventilation and reduced oxygen reserve, plan positioning, and select appropriately sized equipment and drug doses.

blocks.answer: BMI about 35.9 kg/m2: obese; plan for airway, ventilation, sleep apnoea and drug dosing.

blocks.markdown: **The ASA physical status classification (objective 2).** The American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) grade describes the patient's pre-existing systemic health on a scale from I to VI. It is a simple, widely used descriptor and a crude predictor of risk, but it is not a risk score: it does not account for the type of surgery, age or frailty and different assessors may disagree. An 'E' is added for emergency surgery.

rows: I
Normal healthy patient
Fit non-smoker with minimal alcohol use
II
Mild systemic disease
Well-controlled hypertension or diabetes, current smoker, pregnancy, BMI 30 to 40
III
Severe systemic disease
Poorly controlled diabetes or hypertension, COPD, morbid obesity, dialysis-dependent renal failure, stable coronary stents older than 3 months
IV
Severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life
Recent myocardial infarction or stroke, severe valve disease, sepsis, ongoing cardiac ischaemia
V
Moribund patient not expected to survive without the operation
Ruptured aneurysm with shock, massive trauma
VI
Declared brain-dead patient whose organs are being removed for donation
Organ donor
blocks.caption: ASA physical status classification (E added for emergencies). Examples are illustrative and grading depends on clinical judgement.

blocks.title: Assigning ASA grades
blocks.prompt: Grade (A) a 35-year-old fit athlete for an ACL repair; (B) a 61-year-old with COPD, breathless after 100 m on the flat, stable on regular inhalers; (C) a 49-year-old smoker with well-controlled hypertension.

steps.text: A: no systemic disease means ASA I.
B: COPD with significant functional limitation is severe systemic disease that limits activity but is not an immediate threat to life, so ASA III.
C: smoking and well-controlled hypertension are mild systemic disease, so ASA II.
State the limits: ASA grade does not account for the planned surgery, and borderline cases are graded by clinical judgement.

blocks.answer: A is ASA I, B is ASA III and C is ASA II.

blocks.markdown: **Fasting and medicines (objective 3).** Fasting reduces the volume and acidity of gastric contents and so the risk of aspiration after loss of airway reflexes. Commonly applied UK guidance for adult elective surgery is no solid food or non-clear fluids (including milk) for 6 hours, and clear fluids allowed up to 2 hours before anaesthesia; chewing gum and sweets are treated like food. Children and pregnant women have separate protocols, and emergency patients are treated as having a full stomach regardless of fasting time. Prolonged fasting should be avoided because it causes dehydration, hypotension and discomfort. Check against current local guidance.

rows: Beta-blockers, statins, anti-anginals, inhalers, antiepileptics
Continue, including the morning of surgery
Abrupt withdrawal can cause rebound tachycardia, ischaemia, seizures or bronchospasm
Long-term oral corticosteroids
Continue; consider additional perioperative steroid cover
Adrenal suppression can cause hypotension under stress
Anticoagulants and antiplatelets
Plan timing of stopping and restarting individually
Balance bleeding against thrombosis; local protocols and specialist advice
ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics
Practice varies; many units omit on the morning of surgery
Risk of hypotension and acute kidney injury
Diabetes medicines (insulin, SGLT2 inhibitors, others)
Follow specific guidance; insulin is not stopped completely, SGLT2 inhibitors are withheld beforehand
Hypoglycaemia, hyperglycaemia and euglycaemic ketoacidosis
blocks.caption: Examples of perioperative medicine management. Medicine decisions are individual; check the BNF and local guidance.

blocks.title: Planning a fasting time
blocks.prompt: An elective patient ate toast at 08:00 and is next on the list at 13:15. Under a 6 hour rule for solid food, can the anaesthetic start on time, and how long must the team wait?

steps.text: The patient is 45 minutes short of the fasting period, so the start should be delayed until 14:00, or an alternative order of the list considered; clear fluids are still permitted until 2 hours before. Check against current local guidance.

blocks.answer: Not yet: 45 minutes short of 6 hours; wait until 14:00.

blocks.title: Fasting rules do not make the stomach empty
blocks.text: Diabetes, opioids, bowel obstruction, pregnancy, trauma and pain slow gastric emptying. Emergency patients are managed as full stomach, using rapid sequence induction where appropriate.

points: Preoperative assessment identifies risk and allows optimisation, planning and consent; assess airway, functional capacity and comorbidity.
Mallampati class I to IV grades the visible pharyngeal structures; functional capacity of about 4 METs (two flights of stairs) suggests reasonable reserve.
ASA grade I to VI describes pre-existing systemic disease and is a crude risk indicator, not a prediction on its own.

Fasting commonly requires 6 hours for solids and 2 hours for clear fluids; most regular medicines are continued, steroids continued with cover, and anticoagulants, ACE inhibitors and diabetes drugs managed by specific guidance. Check local policy.

questions.stem: At airway assessment a patient sits with mouth fully open and tongue protruded. Only the hard palate can be seen. Which Mallampati class is this?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: only the hard palate is visible.
distractorRationale.b: Class III shows soft palate and the base of the uvula.
distractorRationale.c: Class II shows soft palate, uvula and fauces.
distractorRationale.d: Class I shows soft palate, uvula, fauces and pillars.

questions.explanation: The classes grade how much of the pharynx is visible, from I (nearly everything) to IV (hard palate only). Higher classes predict more difficult laryngoscopy, though the test must be combined with others.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man is asked about exercise tolerance before elective surgery. Which statement best indicates adequate functional capacity?

options.text: He can climb two flights of stairs without stopping (about 4 METs or more)
He drives to the shops daily but never walks
He avoids all stairs because of breathlessness
He walks slowly on the flat but stops after 50 metres

questions.correctOptionText: He can climb two flights of stairs without stopping (about 4 METs or more)

distractorRationale.a: Correct: about 4 METs or more suggests reasonable cardiopulmonary reserve.
distractorRationale.d: This indicates limited reserve and should prompt further assessment.

questions.explanation: Functional capacity is the strongest simple guide to reserve and is taken from what the patient can do. Poor capacity prompts further assessment, such as echocardiography or cardiopulmonary exercise testing for major surgery.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old non-smoker with well-controlled hypertension on one drug and a BMI of 26 kg/m2 is scheduled for a hernia repair. Which ASA grade is most appropriate?

distractorRationale.b: ASA I requires no systemic disease.
distractorRationale.c: ASA IV is a constant threat to life.
distractorRationale.d: ASA III is for severe systemic disease with functional limitation.

questions.explanation: Well-controlled hypertension is an example of mild systemic disease without functional limitation. ASA grading is a judgement of pre-existing health and does not account for the type of surgery.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man with a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm, systolic blood pressure 60 mmHg and loss of consciousness is moribund and will not survive without surgery. How should he be graded?

distractorRationale.a: ASA VI is a declared brain-dead organ donor.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: moribund and not expected to survive without the operation, emergency.
distractorRationale.c: ASA IV is for severe disease that is a constant threat to life but where survival without surgery is expected.
distractorRationale.d: ASA III is for severe disease that is not an immediate threat to life.

questions.explanation: ASA V describes a moribund patient not expected to survive without the operation, and the E suffix denotes emergency surgery. The classification is simple and relies on definitions, so it is applied by clinical judgement.

questions.stem: Which of the following medicines should usually be continued, including on the morning of elective surgery?

options.text: Warfarin with no plan or INR check
An SGLT2 inhibitor taken for diabetes
A long-term beta-blocker taken for angina
A herbal supplement with antiplatelet effects

questions.correctOptionText: A long-term beta-blocker taken for angina

distractorRationale.a: Warfarin needs an individual plan for stopping and INR checking.
distractorRationale.b: SGLT2 inhibitors are withheld before surgery because of the risk of euglycaemic ketoacidosis.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: abrupt withdrawal risks rebound tachycardia and myocardial ischaemia.
distractorRationale.d: Supplements with bleeding effects are usually stopped.

questions.explanation: Drugs whose sudden withdrawal causes harm, such as beta-blockers, are continued perioperatively. Others, like SGLT2 inhibitors and anticoagulants, need specific advance plans; check local guidance.

questions.stem: A patient who has taken oral prednisolone daily for many months should have it stopped before surgery to avoid wound problems.
questions.explanation: Long-term steroids suppress the adrenal axis, so stopping them can cause adrenal insufficiency and hypotension during the stress of surgery. They are continued, and additional perioperative steroid cover is considered according to local guidance.

questions.stem: A patient weighs 105 kg and is 1.75 m tall. Calculate the body mass index in kg/m2, to one decimal place.
questions.explanation: Height squared is 1.75 x 1.75 = 3.0625 m2. BMI is 105 / 3.0625 = 34.3 kg/m2, which is in the obese range and prompts questions about sleep apnoea, reflux and airway difficulty.

questions.stem: An elective patient ate a sandwich at 06:45 and is scheduled for anaesthesia at 12:30. Using a rule of 6 hours without solid food, how many minutes short of the fasting period is the patient? (Enter 0 if the period is already satisfied.)
questions.explanation: From 06:45 to 12:30 is 5 hours 45 minutes, which is 345 minutes. Six hours is 360 minutes, so the patient is 15 minutes short and the start should be delayed or the list reordered; check local policy.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man is listed for a colectomy. He takes a beta-blocker, an ACE inhibitor, metformin and warfarin, and says that he can walk only 50 metres before stopping with breathlessness. Describe how you would assess his cardiorespiratory fitness and outline the perioperative medicine plan and fasting advice.
markingGuide: Functional capacity assessment (METs) and cardiorespiratory history and examination
Further tests as indicated: ECG, echocardiography, cardiopulmonary exercise testing for major surgery
Recognises poor reserve and high risk; plan critical care and consent
ACE inhibitor: practice varies, often omitted morning of surgery

Metformin and warfarin: follow local protocols; plan the INR check before surgery; bridging is not routine and is reserved for patients at high thrombotic risk (e.g. mechanical mitral valve, recent VTE or stroke) per local guidance
Fasting: commonly 6 hours solids and 2 hours clear fluids; check local guidance
questions.explanation: Assessment determines risk and informs where the patient is managed afterwards. Medicine plans are written in advance so that the patient knows what to do on the day.

questions.stem: Describe the components of a preoperative airway assessment and explain why prediction of a difficult airway is imperfect.
markingGuide: History: previous difficulty, sleep apnoea, neck or jaw disease
Mouth opening, dentition, Mallampati class, thyromental distance, mandibular protrusion, neck extension
Combines tests; each has limited sensitivity and specificity
Unanticipated difficulty occurs, so a failed intubation plan must be prepared for every patient
questions.explanation: Individual tests have limited predictive value, so a combination of assessments and a plan prepared for failure is the safe approach.
